items.title: [Comment] Is chemotherapy still needed in all patients with mismatch repair-deficient advanced or recurrent endometrial cancer?
items.summary: Around a quarter of advanced or recurrent endometrial carcinomas are mismatch repair deficient (dMMR).1 Addition of a PD-1 or PD-L1 inhibitor to carboplatin plus paclitaxel has transformed first-line treatment for this subgroup, with the RUBY,1 NRG-GY018,2 AtTEnd,3 and DUO-E4 trials reporting hazard ratios (HRs) for progression-free survival of 0·28–0·42 in their dMMR populations, and 4-year follow-up of RUBY suggests that some patients might be cured.5 However, every one of these trials retained chemotherapy.

items.title: [Comment] The overlooked role of CMV in pneumonia in infants with HIV
items.summary: For decades, severe pneumonia in infants with HIV has been treated as a race against time. Clinicians rapidly initiate broad-spectrum antibiotics, empirically treat suspected Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia, provide supportive care, and increasingly consider empirical tuberculosis treatment in high-burden settings, in line with WHO recommendations.1 Yet mortality remains unacceptably high despite these interventions.2 The EMPIRICAL trial by Cinta Moraleda and colleagues challenges another long-standing assumption; perhaps one important pathogen has been hiding in plain sight.

items.title: [Comment] Empirical tuberculosis treatment in infants living with HIV: missed opportunities and ways to improve outcomes
items.summary: Pneumonia remains the leading cause of death among infants living with HIV, with the case-fatality rate approaching 40%.1 Improving outcomes for these vulnerable infants demands new diagnostic and therapeutic approaches, yet current WHO guidelines for severe pneumonia in this population recommend only empirical coverage of Pneumocystis jirovecii and common bacterial respiratory pathogens.2 In addition, tuberculosis and cytomegalovirus are common causes of severe respiratory disease in infants living with HIV that remain unaddressed by current empirical therapy guidelines.

items.title: [Correspondence] The Perth Declaration to eliminate rheumatic fever and rheumatic heart disease
items.summary: The persistence of rheumatic heart disease reveals how profoundly social inequity can shape who benefits from medical progress. Approximately 55 million people live with the disease, and more than 370 000 die each year.1 It is the most common acquired heart disease in people younger than 25 years, occurring during the years in which these individuals finish their education, form families, and build working lives. Rheumatic heart disease affects women and girls in greater numbers than men and boys,1 and their needs have too often been overlooked.

items.title: [Correspondence] WHO's operational role in emergencies: a view from Gaza

items.title: [Correspondence] Evidence and gaps for preventing postpartum haemorrhage
items.summary: The claim by Ioannis D Gallos and colleagues that tranexamic acid does not have a preventive role does not reflect the scientific evidence.1 The Sustainable Development Goal is to reduce the maternal mortality ratio to fewer than 70 per 100 000 livebirths by 2030.2 Tranexamic acid is the only intervention shown to prevent death from bleeding in randomised trials.3,4 Early administration is most effective. Giving tranexamic acid to all women giving birth would reduce maternal deaths in countries where the risk of maternal death from bleeding is five or more per 100 000 births.

items.title: [Correspondence] Evidence and gaps for preventing postpartum haemorrhage – Authors’ reply

Lieber and colleagues’ comment highlights the importance of distinguishing evidence for prevention from evidence for treatment. We agree with them that tranexamic acid is a life-saving treatment for postpartum haemorrhage and should be given promptly after diagnosis.
